prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling
For the invention of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand breaks

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B011 with Buchwald and Hartwig, and B008 with Liu. The complete round-1 exchange did not weaken either part on scientific grounds; the objections to both are about overlap with earlier prizes and about attribution, not about quality. C-N coupling has the clearest mechanism on the shortlist and thirty years of independent use. Base editing is a defined deaminase chemistry redirected to one nucleotide without a strand break, reproduced widely and already in patients. Together they form two sentences a broad audience can follow, one about making molecules and one about changing a base in DNA, with three people in total. I changed one thing: my alternatives are now B016 and B009 instead of B067 and B043, because after round 1 those two have more committee support than nanopores or perovskites, and I would rather name the realistic fallbacks than my own earlier affinities.
statement.case_against: The weak point is still the uneven pairing. A method from the 1990s and a field in early clinical development are not equally mature, and a single-story prize would be easier to defend. Liu alone omits Komor and Gaudelli, who carried out the cytosine and adenine editor work, and the three-person cap makes that cost explicit. B011 has the 2010 question and a Kosugi precursor to handle in the background text. B008 sits near the 2020 CRISPR prize. No configuration has five votes yet, so if the vote shows B011 alone or B008 alone is closer to a majority, I would accept dropping the weaker part rather than force the pair.

responses.point: Chabes keeps base editing as the sole part with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli, and lists bystander editing, clinical maturity and the Nishida and Kondo work as open points.
responses.response: I take the argument for Komor and Gaudelli seriously: the adenine base editor needed a deaminase that did not exist for DNA, and that evolution was done by Gaudelli. Still, Liu conceived and directed both editor classes, and the three-person cap means adding them costs Hartwig or Buchwald in a pair. I hold Liu alone for the two-part version, but if the vote goes to B008 as a single part, I would support Liu, Komor and Gaudelli without hesitation. On Nishida and Kondo, a concurrent cytidine-deaminase result is worth a mention in the background, not a name, because the programmable adenine editor and the broad generality came from the Liu group.

responses.point: Somfai argues that C-N coupling needed its own ligand and mechanistic solutions and that 2010 laureates did not work on it, while admitting he has not checked priority dates for Kosugi and Migita.
responses.response: This answers my round-1 worry about the 2010 prize, and I now count it as the specialist view. It also supports the citation wording: the claim is generality through ligand control, not the first palladium-mediated C-N bond. I would still ask for the Kosugi and Migita dates to be checked before the vote, so that the background text can say precisely that the tin-amide reaction was a precursor lacking scope. Somfai also asks whether a two-part prize would be better than one topic; my answer is yes only if both parts can be credited without a fourth name, which is why Liu stays alone.

responses.point: Aqvist prefers PROTACs and cereblon glues with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, while acknowledging no degrader is widely approved and the concept and the glue mechanism are different discoveries.
responses.response: His own case against is the strongest one: the lack of an approved degrader and the split between a designed heterobifunctional concept and a mechanism found after the fact mean the citation would be two stories in one sentence. I find the science important and B009 is now my second alternative, but I do not think the committee can defend a three-name cut that leaves out Ciulli, Sakamoto, Ito and Gray before clinical validation exists. If he proposes a narrow PROTAC-only or glue-only citation, I would listen, though that is a different prize from the one he has written.

responses.point: Aili and Sparr prefer ionizable lipid nanoparticles as a single part, arguing the 2023 Medicine prize honoured the cargo and not the delivery chemistry.
responses.response: The clinical validation of B016 is the strongest on the list and I now name it first among my alternatives. The delivery chemistry argument is persuasive. What I cannot resolve is attribution: the third name is Anderson for Aili and Madden for Sparr, with MacLachlan and Langer also credited, and I cannot see an agreed narrow citation in which the three names can be explained by one invention. Until the committee settles who made the decisive step, I cannot rank it above B011 or B008.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a two-part prize of uneven maturity, or whether a majority forms only for B011 or B008 on its own.
How much weight the 2010 and 2020 prizes carry against B011 and B008 respectively.
Whether Liu alone for base editing survives the vote, or the committee insists on Komor and Gaudelli, in which case I would favour B008 as a sole part.
Exact priority dates for Kosugi and Migita relative to Buchwald and Hartwig.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I work in nanophysics at Lund, so I have no stated personal or institutional tie to the laureates in B011, B008, B016 or B009; Somfai and Sparr are Lund colleagues, which is not a conflict for these candidates. I no longer prefer B067, so my earlier field affinity does not affect my position.
